Change Detection on EO Imagery¶

DeepLabV3 vs Simple U-Net vs Siamese U-Net vs ChangeFormer (LEVIR-CD Dataset)¶

Objective¶

This notebook presents a structured comparison of multiple change detection architectures for Earth Observation (EO) imagery.

We evaluate:

  • DeepLabV3-ResNet50 (baseline)
  • Simple U-Net
  • Siamese U-Net (shared encoder, feature-difference fusion)
  • ChangeFormer-B0 (transformer-based)

Goal: understand the trade-offs between classical CNN-based change detection, encoder–decoder architectures, and transformer-based models under a controlled setup.

Workflow¶

  1. Data loading and inspection
  2. Image preprocessing
  3. Model training (4 architectures)
  4. Evaluation and comparison (OA, F1, mIoU)
  5. Prediction visualization

Dataset¶

We use a subset of the LEVIR-CD dataset:

  • high-resolution aerial image pairs (before / after)
  • RGB imagery (bi-temporal observations per sample)
  • pixel-wise binary change masks (change vs. no change)
  • building change detection task
  • strong class imbalance (changed pixels are sparse)
  • resized to a consistent input size

The dataset is split into training, validation, and test sets.

Image Preprocessing¶

Bi-temporal pair preparation (before / after images + change mask)

In [4]:
# Train / Validation / Test split (60 / 20 / 20) on full dataset
indices = list(range(len(ds_all)))
random.shuffle(indices)
n_train = int(0.6*len(indices))
n_val = int(0.2*len(indices))
train_idx, val_idx, test_idx = indices[:n_train], indices[n_train:n_train+n_val], indices[n_train+n_val:]

print(f"Train: {len(train_idx)}, Val: {len(val_idx)}, Test: {len(test_idx)}")

from torchvision import transforms
import torchvision.transforms.functional as TF

tf_img = transforms.Compose([
    transforms.Resize((512, 512)), 
])

# Resize input image pairs (before/after); masks resized with nearest interpolation to preserve labels
class ChangeDataset(torch.utils.data.Dataset):
    def __init__(self, base, indices, tf_img=None, size=512): 
        self.base = base
        self.indices = indices
        self.tf_img = tf_img
        self.size = size

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.indices)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        sample = self.base[self.indices[idx]]
        img1, img2, mask = sample["image"][0], sample["image"][1], sample["mask"][0]

        if isinstance(img1, torch.Tensor):
            img1 = TF.resize(img1, (self.size, self.size))
            img2 = TF.resize(img2, (self.size, self.size))
        if isinstance(mask, torch.Tensor):
            mask = TF.resize(mask.unsqueeze(0), (self.size, self.size), interpolation=TF.InterpolationMode.NEAREST).squeeze(0)

        img = torch.cat([img1, img2], dim=0)  # [6, H, W]
        mask = mask.long()                    # [H, W]

        return img, mask


train_ds = ChangeDataset(ds_all, train_idx, tf_img=tf_img)
val_ds   = ChangeDataset(ds_all, val_idx, tf_img=tf_img)
test_ds  = ChangeDataset(ds_all, test_idx, tf_img=tf_img)

train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=4, shuffle=True)
val_loader   = DataLoader(val_ds, batch_size=4)
test_loader  = DataLoader(test_ds, batch_size=4)

Train: 267, Val: 89, Test: 89

Model training (4 architectures)¶

DeepLabV3-ResNet50 (baseline), Simple U-Net, Siamese U-Net, and ChangeFormer-B0 are trained under a unified pipeline.

In [5]:
# Unified training setup across all architectures for fair comparison 
model_name = "changeformer"   # "deeplabv3" | "unet" | "siamese_unet" | "changeformer"

if model_name == "deeplabv3":
    model = deeplabv3_resnet50(weights=None, num_classes=2)
    model.backbone.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(6, 64, kernel_size=7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False)

elif model_name == "unet":
    model = smp.Unet(
        encoder_name="resnet50",
        encoder_weights=None,
        in_channels=6,
        classes=2
    )

elif model_name == "siamese_unet":
    class SiameseUNet(nn.Module):
        def __init__(self):
            super().__init__()

            base_model = smp.Unet(
                encoder_name="resnet50",
                encoder_weights=None,
                in_channels=3,
                classes=2
            )

            self.encoder = base_model.encoder
            self.decoder = base_model.decoder
            self.segmentation_head = base_model.segmentation_head

        def forward(self, img1, img2):
            feat1 = self.encoder(img1)
            feat2 = self.encoder(img2)

            fused_feats = [torch.abs(f1 - f2) for f1, f2 in zip(feat1, feat2)]

            decoder_output = self.decoder(fused_feats)
            masks = self.segmentation_head(decoder_output)
            return masks

    model = SiameseUNet()

elif model_name == "changeformer":
    model = SegformerForSemanticSegmentation.from_pretrained(
        "nvidia/segformer-b0-finetuned-ade-512-512",
        num_labels=2,
        ignore_mismatched_sizes=True
    )
    model.segformer.encoder.patch_embeddings[0].proj = nn.Conv2d(
        6, 32, kernel_size=7, stride=4, padding=3
    )

model = model.to(device)

criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss(weight=torch.tensor([1.0, 1.5]).to(device))
optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-4)
scheduler = optim.lr_scheduler.StepLR(optimizer, step_size=5, gamma=0.5)

Some weights of SegformerForSemanticSegmentation were not initialized from the model checkpoint at nvidia/segformer-b0-finetuned-ade-512-512 and are newly initialized because the shapes did not match:
- decode_head.classifier.bias: found shape torch.Size([150]) in the checkpoint and torch.Size([2]) in the model instantiated
- decode_head.classifier.weight: found shape torch.Size([150, 256, 1, 1]) in the checkpoint and torch.Size([2, 256, 1, 1]) in the model instantiated
You should probably TRAIN this model on a down-stream task to be able to use it for predictions and inference.
In [6]:
# Handle different output formats across architectures 
def forward_pass(model, imgs, masks=None):
    if model_name == "deeplabv3":
        return model(imgs)["out"]

    elif model_name == "unet":
        return model(imgs)

    elif model_name == "siamese_unet":
        img1 = imgs[:, :3]
        img2 = imgs[:, 3:]
        return model(img1, img2)

    elif model_name == "changeformer":
        out = model(pixel_values=imgs).logits
        if masks is not None:
            out = F.interpolate(out, size=masks.shape[-2:], mode="bilinear", align_corners=False)
        return out


def evaluate(loader):
    model.eval()
    y_true, y_pred = [], []

    with torch.no_grad():
        for imgs, masks in loader:
            imgs, masks = imgs.to(device), masks.to(device)
            out = forward_pass(model, imgs, masks)
            preds = out.argmax(1)

            y_true.extend(masks.cpu().numpy().ravel())
            y_pred.extend(preds.cpu().numpy().ravel())

    y_true, y_pred = np.array(y_true), np.array(y_pred)
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=[0, 1])

    acc = np.diag(cm).sum() / cm.sum()
    iou = np.diag(cm) / (cm.sum(1) + cm.sum(0) - np.diag(cm) + 1e-6)
    f1 = 2 * np.diag(cm) / (cm.sum(1) + cm.sum(0) + 1e-6)

    return acc, iou, f1


EPOCHS = 20
best_miou = 0.0
best_path = f"best_{model_name}_levircd.pth"

for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    model.train()
    losses = []

    for imgs, masks in train_loader:
        imgs, masks = imgs.to(device), masks.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        out = forward_pass(model, imgs, masks)
        loss = criterion(out, masks)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        losses.append(loss.item())

    # Validation 
    val_acc, val_iou, val_f1 = evaluate(val_loader)
    miou = val_iou.mean()

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{EPOCHS}, "
        f"Loss={np.mean(losses):.4f}, "
        f"Val OA={val_acc:.4f}, mIoU={miou:.4f}, F1={val_f1.mean():.4f}"
    )

    if miou > best_miou:
        best_miou = miou

        # Optional: save best model checkpoint
        # Disabled by default to avoid unintended overwrites during repeated experiments
        
        # torch.save(model.state_dict(), best_path)
        # print(f"Saved new best model: {best_path} (mIoU={best_miou:.4f})")

    scheduler.step()

Experimental Notes¶

Several factors were evaluated to identify what drives change detection performance.

  • Optimizer and LR tuning showed no meaningful improvement. Changing Adam to AdamW/SGD and varying learning rates did not improve performance → baseline already well-tuned.
  • StepLR provided minor improvement in change-class F1/IoU, while cosine decay did not → stable convergence matters more than schedule complexity.
  • Class weighting is critical. Moderate weighting (~1.5) improves detection; under-weighting increases FN, over-weighting increases FP.
  • Data augmentation was generally harmful. RandomCrop removes spatial context; horizontal flipping provides limited benefit due to inherent orientation invariance in aerial imagery; ColorJitter introduces false change signals → consistency is more important than diversity.
  • Model complexity does not ensure improvement. Simple U-Net performs competitively due to strong spatial detail preservation, while Siamese U-Net provides no benefit over simple concatenation.
  • Transformer-based models (ChangeFormer) achieve strong peak performance but do not show consistent advantage in limited-data settings.
  • Increasing resolution (256 → 512) improves performance across models, with the largest gain in DeepLabV3 due to multi-scale context modeling (ASPP). Higher resolution provides larger effective context, improving detection of small or spatially scattered building changes.
  • Longer training gives diminishing returns. 10 → 30 epochs improves slightly but increases cost.
  • Overall, performance is driven by spatial context and class imbalance handling, rather than optimizer choice or architectural complexity.

Visualization¶

In [8]:
# Prediction visualization on test samples
model.eval()

show_indices = [7, 10, 46, 82]  # representative samples (fixed for comparison)
N = len(show_indices)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(N, 5, figsize=(9, 1.75 * N))

for row, idx in enumerate(show_indices):
    img, mask = test_ds[idx]

    with torch.no_grad():
        imgs = img.unsqueeze(0).to(device)
        mask_t = mask.unsqueeze(0).to(device)
        pred = forward_pass(model, imgs, mask_t).argmax(1).squeeze().cpu().numpy()

    mask = mask.numpy()
    img1 = img[:3].permute(1, 2, 0).numpy()
    img2 = img[3:].permute(1, 2, 0).numpy()

    # TP / FP / FN
    tp = (pred == 1) & (mask == 1)
    fp = (pred == 1) & (mask == 0)
    fn = (pred == 0) & (mask == 1)

    overlay = np.zeros((*pred.shape, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
    overlay[tp] = [0, 255, 0] # Green = True Positive
    overlay[fp] = [255, 0, 0] # Red = False Positive
    overlay[fn] = [0, 0, 255] # Blue = False Negative

    axes[row, 0].imshow(img1.astype(np.uint8))
    axes[row, 1].imshow(img2.astype(np.uint8))
    axes[row, 2].imshow(mask, cmap="gray")
    axes[row, 3].imshow(pred, cmap="gray")
    axes[row, 4].imshow(overlay)
    
    for col in range(5):
        axes[row, col].axis("off")

titles = ["Before", "After", "GT", "Pred", "TP (G) / FP (R) / FN (B)"]
for col in range(5):
    axes[0, col].set_title(titles[col], fontsize=11)

plt.tight_layout(pad=0.5, w_pad=0.0, h_pad=1.0)
plt.show()

Model captures large structures reliably; errors concentrate on thin boundaries and fragmented changes.

Model Comparison¶

Model Input Size OA mIoU Mean F1 Strength Limitation
DeepLabV3 256×256 0.96 0.69 0.78 Strong multi-scale context modeling (ASPP) Sensitive to resolution (weaker at lower resolution)
DeepLabV3 512×512 0.98 0.77 0.86 Effective context aggregation at higher resolution Higher computational cost
Simple U-Net 256×256 0.97 0.69 0.79 Stable baseline, strong spatial detail preservation Limited global context
Simple U-Net 512×512 0.97 0.75 0.84 Improved spatial detail with higher resolution Limited global context
Siamese U-Net 256×256 0.96 0.64 0.73 Explicit temporal comparison No gain over simple concatenation
Siamese U-Net 512×512 0.97 0.70 0.79 Explicit temporal comparison No gain over simple concatenation
ChangeFormer-B0 256×256 0.97 0.70 0.80 Global context modeling (transformer) Limited data efficiency / inconsistent gains in small data
ChangeFormer-B0 512×512 0.98 0.78 0.86 Strong global context modeling at higher resolution Higher complexity with limited consistency gains

Key Observations

  • Performance depends on architecture–resolution interaction, not model complexity alone
  • U-Net remains competitive at 256×256 due to spatial detail preservation
  • DeepLabV3 benefits significantly from higher resolution via multi-scale context modeling
  • Siamese design provides no advantage over simple input concatenation
  • ChangeFormer-B0 achieves the best results at 512×512, but without consistent gains relative to its complexity
  • Change-class metrics (F1/IoU) reveal differences more clearly than OA under class imbalance

Conclusion¶

  • Simple U-Net is a reliable baseline, particularly at lower resolution
  • DeepLabV3 scales effectively with resolution due to context aggregation
  • ChangeFormer-B0 achieves the highest performance, but with higher complexity and limited consistency across settings
  • Errors concentrate on thin boundaries and fragmented changes, while large structures are reliably detected
  • Performance gains are primarily driven by spatial context aggregation (especially at higher resolution) and class imbalance handling, rather than architectural complexity

This study shows that, under limited-data conditions, improvements come from effective context use and balanced loss design, while more complex architectures provide only marginal or inconsistent benefits relative to their cost.
